headlines.article_text: CFTC investigates if Kalshi improperly self-certified event contracts Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Kalshi called it a minor issue in how the contracts were filed and said it is working with the CFTC to address the matter. Prediction market platforms are allowed to self-certify event contracts without the federal agency's approval, as long as they comply with the Commodity Exchange Act. A Kalshi billboard displaying US Congress midterm election odds in New York, US, on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. Angelina Katsanis | Bloomberg | Getty Images The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is investigating whether prediction market platform Kalshi failed to properly inform the agency of proposed event contracts, Kalshi confirmed to CNBC. Kalshi called it a minor issue in how the contracts were filed and said it is working with the CFTC to address the matter. The CFTC flagged weather-related contracts, Kalshi said. The leading prediction market platform didn't say when the agency began investigating Kalshi. CFTC Chairman Michael Selig told CNBC that the agency does not comment on investigations. Politico first reported on the probe on Tuesday, noting charges could happen soon, based on the CFTC's private notification to Kalshi. The platform declined to comment on any possible charges. Prediction market platforms are allowed to self-certify event contracts without the federal agency's prior approval, as long as they comply with the Commodity Exchange Act. The self-certification allows for faster introduction of new contracts. 'Procedural error' "The notice is about a procedural error involving the submission of a handful of contracts, many of which weren't live," said Elisabeth Diana, head of communications at Kalshi. "We are already addressing the issue." The move is the latest by the CFTC as it seeks to rein in prediction markets, which face growing scrutiny in Washington from regulators and members of Congress . In August, the CFTC ordered Kalshi to take down sports-related " mention markets " — where speculators can trade on what individuals will say in a broadcast or speech — while it looked into the event contract type. The agency is also conducting a broad probe into competitor Polymarket , which includes reviewing if the company violated a 2022 settlement with the CFTC to prohibit U.S. traders from accessing its international trading platform. Polymarket's domestic exchange operates separately from the global platform. Prediction markets are also expected to face heightened scrutiny once the Democratic Congress is sworn into office in January. Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., in a Tuesday social media post on X , called for a ban on sports prediction markets — which account for the overwhelming majority of volume on leading platforms. — CNBC's Talia Kaplan contributed to this report Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment. headlines.article_text: Meta head of infrastructure will depart, succeeded by former AWS exec Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Meta's head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering Santosh Janardhan will leave in 2027. Janardhan's successor, former AWS senior vice president David Brown, will lead Meta's infrastructure efforts of the Meta Compute initiative, spearheaded by Dina Powell McCormick and Daniel Gross. The executive move underscores Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg's efforts to expand the company's data center operations under newer leaders at a time of increasing investor scrutiny on capital expenditure spending by the social media giant and its hyperscaler rivals. In this article META Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Santosh Janardhan, head of infrastructure at Meta Platforms Inc., speaks during the Arm Everywhere event in San Francisco, California, US, on Tuesday, March 24, 2026. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images Meta's long-time infrastructure leader will leave the company in the new year, setting the stage for a recently hired former Amazon Web Services executive to oversee its massive data center technical operations. Santosh Janardhan, Meta's head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering, revealed his upcoming departure on Wednesday in an internal memo obtained by CNBC. Janardhan, who has worked at Meta since 2009, said "it's time to pass the baton" to former AWS senior vice president David Brown, who joined Meta in July from AWS. The executive move underscores Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg's efforts to expand the company's data center operations under newer leaders at a time of increasing investor scrutiny on capital expenditure spending by the social media giant and its hyperscaler rivals. Brown will now formally lead Meta's infrastructure efforts as part of the Meta Compute initiative, which is spearheaded by the company's president and vice chairman Dina Powell McCormick and technical leader Daniel Gross. Zuckerberg is relying on these new executives to continue developing cutting-edge data centers and related infrastructure needed to support its AI ambitions. The company said during its recent third-quarter earnings report that it expects full-year capex to fall in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion. Meta also logged negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, which S&P Global Ratings noted as part of its decision in late October to revise Meta's credit rating from AA- stable to AA- negative. Janardhan said in the memo that he will help support Brown through the first quarter of 2027 as part of "the transition." "As we make the next set of choices about our priorities, this is the right time for Dave to take the lead in shaping that work," Janardhan said in the memo. "Dave has spent his career building and operating dependable infrastructure for a wide range of demanding workloads. He has the instincts, depth and judgment this moment requires." Bloomberg News first reported on the executive transition.
